objectives: Produce simple spoken CVC words after hearing their phonemes.
Use a consistent hear-join-say strategy without guessing.
concepts: Oral blending joins phonemes in sequence to form a spoken word.
The learner should hear the complete sequence before producing the whole word.
Continuous consonants such as /m/ and /s/ can be stretched briefly to support smooth joining.

definitions.definition: Joining separately spoken phonemes to say a whole word.
A simple word with a consonant, vowel and consonant sound pattern.

commonMistakes: Guessing before hearing the final sound.
Adding an extra vowel after a consonant.
Changing the order of the sounds.
keyTakeaways: Join the sounds and say the whole word.

conceptual: Explain why the sound sequence must stay in order.
Identify the difference between blending and guessing.
application: Blend spoken sounds and choose the matching picture.
Blend the same word a second time more smoothly.
higherOrderThinking: Identify where a learner broke a three-sound blend.
Choose the best support for a learner who adds 'uh' after consonants.
mixedReview: Mix sound sequence, word identity and blending strategy.

formulaOrFactBank: CVC blending: first sound + middle sound + final sound → whole word
mistakeBasedRevision: If the learner guesses early, require all sounds first.
If the learner adds vowels, model smoother continuous joining.
weakTopicRevision: Practise ten familiar CVC blends and repeat any missed sequence.

activities.name: Sound train
steps: Learner joins the sounds and says the word.

activities.name: Blend and choose
steps: Present two or three picture choices.
Learner blends and chooses the matching meaning.

outcomes: Learner orally blends at least 8 of 10 familiar three-phoneme sequences correctly.
Learner maintains phoneme order in at least 8 of 10 attempts.
Learner produces the whole word without an added vowel in at least 8 of 10 attempts.

questions.question: What should you do before saying the whole word?
Why must the sounds stay in order?
options: The order helps form the correct word

questions.question: A learner says 'muh-a-tuh'. What is the best support?
Which learner is blending correctly?
options: Learner A hears all three sounds and says the word
Learner B guesses after one sound
Learner C changes the sound order
Learner D skips the final sound

questions.question: What is the final sound in 'sat'?
What is the first sound in 'tap'?
What is the middle sound in 'mat'?
Which word can be made from /s/ /a/ /t/?
What is oral blending?
options: Joining spoken sounds into a whole word

questions.question: What should you do if your first blend does not sound right?
options: Listen again and keep the sounds in order
